newsitem.title: FRANCE: Council of Europe deputies worried by CIS refugees.
newsitem.headline: Council of Europe deputies worried by CIS refugees.

text.p: The Council of Europe said on Tuesday it was worried about the fate of millions of refugees driven from their homes in parts of the former Soviet Union by armed conflict, environmental crisis or economic necessity.

The council's Parliamentary Assembly urged the former Soviet states -- most of which are now grouped in the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) -- to adopt legislation guaranteeing the rights of refugees and asylum-seekers.

In two reports approved on Tuesday, the parliamentarians also urged the CIS states to "contribute generously to the financing of assistance programmes for refugees, asylum-seekers and displaced persons".
The United Nations refugee agency UNHCR has estimated there are nine million refugees in the CIS.

The reports presented to the assembly by Russian deputy Vadim Fililmonov said the main factors were armed conflicts in Chechnya, Tajikistan and Moldova, regional economic crises and environmental disasters like the Chernobyl nuclear catastrophe or the dying Aral Sea.
"CIS states do not have a grand tradition of welcoming refugees," one of the reports said.
In most former Soviet states, refugees are granted discretionary residence permits which slap conditions on economic and social rights, it said.
Only Armenia, Azerbaijan, Russia and Tajikistan have signed the Geneva convention protecting refugees.
"The remaining states have not done so primarily because difficult social and economic conditions prevent them from assuming their responsibilities," Fililmonov said.

While their lack of action was not justified by these difficulties, the 40 member states of the Council of Europe should do all they could to help the former Soviet states overcome these challenges, he said.

The assembly urged Georgia, Armenia and Azerbaijan, where armed conflicts have created an estimated one million refugees, to make the return of displaced persons a top priority in future negotiations.
It blamed environmental disasters for displacing an estimated 600,000 people.
The council was set up after World War Two to foster democracy and human rights across Europe.
